clue.text: Just the opposite to quick profit

definitions.text: Just the opposite to quick profit

parts.note: surface reading: money made fast, as from a speedy deal
setter's reading: quick is the old word for living, so its opposite is lifeless, and the opposite of profit is a deficit

explanation.surface: A trader ruefully describes a deal that went the wrong way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Quick' means alive, as in 'the quick and the dead', so flipping both words of 'quick profit' gives the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A total write-off brings nothing but waste, the reverse in both halves of a living gain.

clue.text: Issued odd reason for scrapping

indicators.note: odd here means strange or peculiar, so the letters are set in an unusual arrangement

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: An official notice gives a strange justification for throwing something away.
explanation.definitionFit: Equipment left unused for long enough is typically thrown out, so neglect of use is a cause of junking it.

clue.text: Could Midas have been described as one?

definitions.text: Could Midas have been described as one?

parts.note: surface reading: the legendary king whose touch turned everything to gold
setter's reading: the practitioner of the medieval art that sought to turn base metals into gold

explanation.walkthrough: Midas did by touch exactly what the medieval experimenters tried to do in their laboratories.
explanation.definitionFit: Alchemy was the pursuit of transmuting lead and other base metals into gold, which Midas managed effortlessly.

clue.text: It's reached at the end of a flight

definitions.text: It's reached at the end of a flight

parts.note: surface reading: an aeroplane journey finishing on the runway
setter's reading: the level platform you arrive at after climbing a flight of stairs

explanation.walkthrough: Both readings work: a plane touches down at the end of its flight, and a staircase's flight ends at a flat platform.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names both an aircraft touching ground and the platform between or atop stair sections.

clue.text: It's difficult when' so badly scared

definitions.meaning: first meaning: hard, as in a tough exam

definitions.note: completes the phrase with 'scared', meaning frightened to an extreme degree
definitions.meaning: second meaning: the word that follows scared in the idiom for being terrified

explanation.surface: Someone admits a task is hard when nerves have taken hold.
explanation.walkthrough: The stray apostrophe after 'when' is a printing slip in the original.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective means hard or demanding, and in the idiom 'scared stiff' it intensifies fright to paralysis.

clue.text: Bark causes a conspirator to change sex

indicators.note: a man's Latin name made feminine swaps its masculine ending for the female one

parts.note: Cassius was one of the conspirators who assassinated Julius Caesar

explanation.surface: A tree's bark has the bizarre power to turn a plotter into a woman.
explanation.walkthrough: Latin -US is a masculine ending and -A its feminine counterpart, so the plotter's name becomes CASSIA.
explanation.definitionFit: Cassia is the aromatic bark of a tree related to cinnamon, used as a spice.

clue.text: One entitled to an army coat?

definitions.text: One entitled to an army coat?

parts.note: surface reading: a soldier's uniform greatcoat
setter's reading: arm-y as in heraldic arms, so a person granted the right to a coat of arms

explanation.walkthrough: Read 'army' as 'of arms': the coat is a heraldic one, and the answer is a person entitled to bear it.
explanation.definitionFit: An armiger is a heraldic term for a person legally entitled to bear a coat of arms.

clue.text: "My hat!" the old soldier might have said

definitions.text: "My hat!" the old soldier might have said

parts.note: surface reading: an old-fashioned exclamation of surprise

parts.words: the old soldier might have said
parts.note: setter's reading: a veteran naming his own headgear, the tall plumed military cap of the nineteenth century

explanation.walkthrough: 'My hat!' is an exclamation, but taken literally it is a soldier pointing to his cylindrical peaked cap.
explanation.definitionFit: A shako is a tall cylindrical military cap with a peak and plume, worn by soldiers in the 1800s.

clue.text: After the Accounts examination I get on with the hearing

parts.note: an audit is an official inspection of financial accounts
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: After the auditors have finished, someone moves on to a court hearing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hearing' suggests a court case, but here it is a performer's tryout.
explanation.definitionFit: An audition is a trial performance, a hearing given to a singer or actor seeking a role.

clue.text: Exclusively Sassenach?

parts.note: surface reading: the Scots word for an English person, so something purely English
setter's reading: containing no Scotsman at all, which as an idiom means getting away unpunished

explanation.walkthrough: Sassenach is the Scottish word for an English person; something wholly English is free of Scots, which puns on the idiom for escaping without penalty.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom means escaping without paying or being punished, but literally reads as having no Scot in it.

clue.text: His authority seems momentary

parts.note: surface reading: someone whose power is fleeting
setter's reading: a second is a moment, so the officer who holds the deputy's power

explanation.walkthrough: A second is a moment of time, so a deputy's command sounds as if it lasts only an instant.
explanation.definitionFit: The deputy commander ranks just below the chief and takes charge when the leader is absent.

clue.text: She precedes half the rabble in an official capacity

indicators.note: only one of two equal portions is kept, the rest is discarded

parts.note: taken as written
riffraff is a disparaging term for the common mob

explanation.surface: A woman goes ahead of the mob, acting in some formal role.
explanation.walkthrough: Riffraff splits neatly into two equal halves, so 'half the rabble' keeps the first of them.
explanation.definitionFit: A sheriff is a county or town law-enforcement officer, an appointed public functionary.

clue.text: An example of drawing craft

parts.note: surface reading: the artistic skill of sketching
setter's reading: a vessel that draws, that is hauls or tows, other ships

explanation.walkthrough: 'Drawing' suggests sketching and 'craft' a skill, but here a craft is a boat and drawing means pulling.
explanation.definitionFit: A small powerful harbour vessel pulls larger ships, so it is a boat that tows.

clue.text: Odd number, grammatically

definitions.meaning: second meaning: in grammar, the number category for one rather than many

explanation.walkthrough: 'Odd number' reads as one phrase, like three or five, but it splits into two separate meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective means strange or unusual, and in grammar names the form denoting one, opposed to plural.

clue.text: A Greek who had little to say for himself

definitions.text: A Greek who had little to say for himself

parts.words: had little to say for himself
parts.note: surface reading: a quiet, uncommunicative person
setter's reading: a native of the Spartan region, whose people were famous for terse speech

explanation.walkthrough: Laconia was the region around Sparta, whose people were proverbially terse; the word laconic comes from them.
explanation.definitionFit: The Spartans of this region were renowned for brief, pithy speech, giving English the word laconic.

clue.text: Ten to one perhaps — the end of Nelson?

indicators.note: only the closing part of the name is kept, its opening letters being cut away

parts.note: Admiral Lord Nelson's first name was Horatio

explanation.surface: Betting odds of ten to one, perhaps on the death of the famous admiral.
explanation.walkthrough: Drop HO from the front of Horatio to keep its end, RATIO.
explanation.definitionFit: Ten to one expresses a proportion between two quantities, the mathematical relation written 10:1.

clue.text: His examination results make things go to pot

definitions.text: His examination results make things go to pot

parts.note: surface reading: ruin everything, as a disastrous inspection might
setter's reading: a professional sampler whose verdict decides which leaves go into the brewing vessel

explanation.walkthrough: 'Go to pot' means fall apart, but literally the leaves he approves go into the teapot.
explanation.definitionFit: This professional samples brews to grade leaf quality and choose blends for sale.

clue.text: A bird in uniform

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a large Asian stork with a stiff, military gait

definitions.note: a person in uniform: a military officer
definitions.meaning: second meaning: an army officer who assists a commander with administration

explanation.surface: A bird dressed up in a soldier's uniform.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names both a large Indian stork and a staff officer helping a commanding officer with administration.

clue.text: Fruit gets cut of fashion

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the sweet brown fruit of the palm

definitions.note: 'cut' is a printing slip for 'out': becomes outmoded
definitions.meaning: second meaning: becomes old-fashioned, as a style does over time

explanation.walkthrough: 'Cut' is a typesetting error for 'out' in the original paper.
explanation.definitionFit: The palm yields sweet brown fruit, and a style that looks old-fashioned is said to become stale over time.

clue.text: Where to see a bird on the water

indicators.note: in a down clue one thing sitting on another is placed above it, so it comes first

parts.note: a large white water bird
the sea is a body of water

explanation.surface: Directions to a spot for birdwatching on a lake or coast.
explanation.walkthrough: Swansea is a city on the coast of south Wales.
explanation.definitionFit: The clue's opening word asks for a place, and this Welsh port city is that location.

clue.text: One whose activities are always above-board

definitions.text: One whose activities are always above-board

parts.note: surface reading: an honest person who never cheats
setter's reading: a game piece that moves only on top of the checkered playing surface

explanation.walkthrough: 'Above-board' means honest, but a game piece literally moves above the board.
explanation.definitionFit: Kings, pawns, rooks and the rest are pieces that only ever move on top of the chequered surface.

clue.text: Refuse to give old Bob the dregs

parts.note: a bob was a shilling in old British money, abbreviated s
ullage is the residue or dregs left in a cask

explanation.surface: A refusal to hand an old man called Bob anything but the leftovers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Refuse' looks like a verb but is the noun meaning rubbish; a bob was a pre-decimal British shilling, written s.
explanation.definitionFit: Sullage is waste water, sewage or filth, which is rubbish in the sense of discarded matter.

clue.text: The third is a questionable procedure

definitions.text: The third is a questionable procedure

parts.note: surface reading: the third item in some series
setter's reading: a harsh interrogation, literally full of questions, and of dubious propriety

explanation.walkthrough: 'The third degree' is the idiom for intense interrogation, and 'questionable' means both dubious and involving questions.
explanation.definitionFit: The third degree is rough police grilling, so the missing word completes the idiom for it.

clue.text: At least it won't run people down

definitions.text: At least it won't run people down

parts.note: surface reading: it won't criticise anyone, or won't knock anyone over
setter's reading: a railway service heading towards the capital, which therefore never carries passengers in the other direction

explanation.walkthrough: In British railway usage, trains to London run 'up' and away from it 'down'; this one only takes people up.
explanation.definitionFit: On British railways a service travelling towards the capital or main terminus is called up, the opposite of down.

clue.text: Palatine sense?

parts.note: surface reading: relating to a palatinate or count palatine, a historical noble title
setter's reading: the faculty that belongs to the palate, the roof of the mouth

explanation.walkthrough: Palatine usually refers to a royal palace or count, but also means of the palate, the seat of flavour.
explanation.definitionFit: The faculty of perceiving flavour lives in the mouth, the one of five senses linked with the palate.

clue.text: Distance along a motorway, by a wild eagle

parts.note: the M1 is Britain's first major motorway, with the 1 read as the letter I

indicators.note: wild means out of control, so these letters run free into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A distance marker on a motorway beside which a wild eagle is spotted.
explanation.walkthrough: The M1 is the motorway running from London to Leeds; its 1 doubles as the letter I.
explanation.definitionFit: Mileage is a length travelled or covered, counted in miles.

clue.text: In a few words, what's Tom up to

indicators.note: in a down clue, going up means reading the letters from the bottom to the top

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Asking someone to explain briefly what Tom is doing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Up to' looks like a phrase about mischief, but 'up' acts on Tom alone and 'to' is taken literally.
explanation.definitionFit: A motto is a short saying or maxim adopted as a guiding principle, a brief phrase.

clue.text: Head-support

parts.note: surface reading: the head on your shoulders, as a pillow or neck brace holds it
setter's reading: a teacher who helps the headmaster run the school

explanation.walkthrough: The head is the headmaster, and the support is a male schoolteacher working beneath him.
explanation.definitionFit: In older British schools a male teacher on the staff below the head was given this title.

clue.text: The banjoist had no support in Greece

definitions.note: a person from a city in Greece

indicators.note: having none of something means it is taken away from what remains

parts.note: taken as written; that the answer runs across these words is no coincidence, but it is reached by removing the support rather than as a hidden word
a joist is a supporting beam in a floor or ceiling

explanation.surface: A banjo player in Greece found himself without backing.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove JOIST from the end of THE BANJOIST to leave THEBAN.
explanation.definitionFit: A Theban is a native of Thebes, the ancient Greek city in Boeotia.

clue.text: It might indicate a good standard or horticulture.

definitions.text: It might indicate a good standard or horticulture.

parts.note: surface reading: a high level of quality in gardening
setter's reading: a standard is a flowering shrub grafted on a tall single stem, giving a bloom-topped trunk

explanation.walkthrough: A standard in gardening is a plant trained on one tall stem; 'or' is a printing slip for 'of'.
explanation.definitionFit: Gardeners graft the bushes onto a single upright stem so they grow like small trunks with a flowered crown.
